item.title: Opening a business in Aargau: trade register and costs
item.description: Legal forms, registration in the commercial register, minimum capital, taxes and tax obligations in the Canton of Aargau: operational guide.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Mandatory registration with the commercial register within 20 days of starting activity - Legal forms: sole proprietorship, general partnership, SA, Sàrl, cooperative society - Minimum capital: zero for sole proprietorship; CHF 20,000 for Sàrl; CHF 100,000 for SA - Three tax levels: federal (IFD, VAT), cantonal and municipal (Aargau) - Social security obligations (AVS/AI/IPG) and health insurance (LAMal) for employees
## Key facts - **What**: Registration of a company with the Aargau cantonal commercial register - When: Within 20 days of starting the activity - Where: Office of the commercial register of the Canton of Aargau (cantonal administration) - Who: Any natural or legal person starting a commercial activity - Regulatory levels: Federal, cantonal and municipal (three parallel tax systems)
Opening a business in the Canton of Aargau means navigating a three-tier system: federal legislation sets the general framework (legal forms, registration requirements, VAT, AVS), while the Canton and individual municipalities of Aargau define their taxes and administrative procedures.
The choice of legal form is the first fork. A sole proprietorship is the simplest and most direct solution: no minimum capital required, streamlined administration, taxation on the entrepreneur's person. It does, however, involve unlimited liability: creditors can act on the personal assets. General partnerships (Snc) and limited partnerships (Sas) partially limit the liability of the partners, but remain complex. Public limited companies (SA) and limited liability companies (Sàrl) offer capital protection and limited liability, but require minimum capital: CHF 100,000 for the SA (payable in installments: at least 20% at the time of foundation, therefore CHF 20,000), CHF 20,000 for the Sàrl.
Registration with the commercial register is mandatory and must take place within 20 days of starting the activity. Without registration, the company does not have full legal capacity. The Aargau commercial register office will communicate all registration taxes, which vary by legal form. Cantonal and municipal taxes of the Aargau territory will then be calculated on the net income of the company once operational.
Every company in Switzerland with turnover above the threshold (currently around CHF 100,000 annually, subject to revisions) must register for VAT with the Federal Customs Administration. VAT is paid periodically according to the regime (normal, simplified or flat rate according to volume).
If the company employs staff, social security obligations automatically apply: AVS/AI/IPG at 10.6% total (5.3% employee + 5.3% employer), accident insurance LAINF/LAA with percentages varying by sector (0.7-1.5% of salary), and for employees with coordinated salary above the threshold, the obligation to register the company with a pension fund (LPP/BVG) for the second pillar.
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and therefore for every employee in Aargau. It is not a tax: it is a private policy with per capita premiums that vary by canton, region of residence within the canton and deductible class (from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 for adults). Aargau provides premium subsidies for low incomes, managed by the cantonal administration.
[Use the tax calculator to estimate your federal tax burden](nav:calculator) ### The three-tier tax system When opening a business in Aargau, the tax burden is structured in three independent levels. At the federal level, the federal direct tax (IFD) is calculated progressively on net income. There is no single national rate: each canton applies its own multipliers to the federal base. At the cantonal level, Aargau has its own tax laws on business income and capital. At the municipal level, Aargau municipalities add multipliers to the cantonal base, creating variability even within the canton. This means that a company in Baden has a different tax rate than one in Aarau, both in Aargau. For VAT, the threshold and regime depend on the total turnover. If the annual turnover reaches CHF 100,000, mandatory registration in the federal VAT system with the Federal Customs Administration is triggered. The gross amounts on invoices are indicated with VAT, and the standard rate is 8.1% (with reductions for food and media). The company pays the difference between VAT collected and VAT paid on purchases. ### Pension obligations: AHV, BVG, and accident insurance For employees, the Aargau entrepreneur must pay AHV/AI/IV contributions (old-age/invalidity/loss of earnings compensation). The employee pays 5.3% of the gross salary, the employer pays an additional 5.3%, for a total of 10.6%. This contribution is paid to the AHV compensation fund of the canton of Aargau. The self-employed person (independent worker) pays 10.6% directly on the net professional income. For the second pillar (BVG/BVG), every employee with an annual coordinated gross salary (after deduction of a threshold of approximately CHF 884 per month) above CHF 21,150 must be registered with a professional pension fund. Contributions vary by age class: 7% between 25-34 years, 10% between 35-44, 15% between 45-54, 18% from 55 years until the reference age (currently 65 for men, 64 for women). It is the employer's responsibility to register the company with a fund and pay the contributions, which can be partially deducted from cantonal tax. Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) covers occupational accidents and occupational diseases. The contribution is the employer's responsibility (the employee pays nothing) and is a percentage of the salary, varying by economic sector: from 0.7% for offices to 1.5% for high-risk sectors. The payment is made to the cantonal accident insurer or a private entity. ### Health insurance: mandatory LAMal and cantonal subsidies Every employee in Aargau must be registered with health insurance (LAMal/KVG). Unlike pension contributions, LAMal is not a tax or salary contribution: it is a private insurance policy taken out by the individual with an insurer. Premiums are per capita and vary by three factors: canton (Aargau has its own average regional premiums), region of residence within the canton (e.g., urban vs. rural area), and chosen deductible class (CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, 2,500). An employee with a CHF 300 deductible pays a different monthly premium than one with a CHF 2,500 deductible. It is common practice for the employer to pay a flat-rate contribution towards the employees' premiums, but this is not legally required. Aargau, like many cantons, grants premium subsidies to residents with low incomes. The amount of the subsidy depends on the family income and the number of dependents. The application must be submitted to the cantonal administration of Aargau. ### Comparative scenarios: Aargau vs. other cantons An entrepreneur comparing the tax burden between cantons will find substantial differences. Cantons like Uri and Valais have lower rates but fewer public services. Zurich and Geneva have higher rates. Aargau is positioned in the national mid-range, with internal variability according to municipalities. An Aargau tax consultant is essential to quantify the exact taxes in your specific area.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step by step: how to register with the commercial register
The process of registering with the commercial register of Aargau follows a standardized procedure, but the times and fees vary by canton.
Phase 1: Choice of legal form
Decide between a sole proprietorship (very simple, no capital), a partnership (Snc, Sas, medium cost and complexity) or a corporation (SA, Sàrl, with minimum capital but legal protection). The choice affects taxation, liability, administration and management of partners/shareholders. For a sole proprietorship, nothing is needed except a clear vision of your activity. For SA or Sàrl, prepare the articles of association and bylaws according to the official federal models.
**Phase 2: Gathering documentation**
For a sole proprietorship: valid ID (passport or ID card), address of residence or business location in Aargau, any professional licenses required by the sector (e.g., real estate agent, auditor). For SA/Sàrl: articles of association and bylaws signed by all founders, list of names and addresses of all partners/managers, bank certificate attesting the deposit of the minimum capital (20% for SA, 100% for Sàrl). All documents must comply with the official Swiss models and be written in an official language (Italian, German, French).
Phase 3: Submission to the commercial register
Contact the commercial register office of the Canton of Aargau (part of its cantonal administration). Many cantons allow pre-registration and online submission. Submit (or upload) all the prepared documentation. The office will review it and inform you if any additions are needed. Registration must take place within 20 days of the start of the activity: beyond this deadline, the owner risks penalties and loss of certainty about the official start date.
Phase 4: Payment of registration fees
The cantonal administration will communicate the total amount of the registration fees for the commercial register. This amount varies by canton, legal form, and sometimes by estimated turnover. Pay according to the instructions, usually by transferring to a government bank account.
Phase 5: Federal tax registration (VAT)
If the expected turnover exceeds CHF 100,000 annually, contact the Federal Customs Administration (AFD) to register for the VAT system. Registration is mandatory and takes place online. The AFD will assign you a unique VAT number (VAT identification number CHE-XXX.XXX.XXX). From that moment, every invoice must show the calculated VAT.
Phase 6: Registration with the cantonal tax administration
Contact the tax office of the Canton of Aargau (domain office) to register for the cantonal tax system on income and capital. You will provide data about your company: form, location, economic sector, estimated turnover. You will be assigned cantonal identification numbers and deadlines for annual declarations (usually by March 31 of the following year of the tax period).
Phase 7: Social security registration (AVS/AI/IPG)
If you are not already an employee of someone else, contact the AVS compensation body of your Aargau region to register as a self-employed worker. You will pay AVS/AI/IPG contributions on 92% of your net professional income, at a total of 10.6%. If you hire employees, communicate their data and salaries to the AVS body, which will manage the payroll deductions (pay slip).
Phase 8: Pension fund (LPP) and accident insurance (LAA)
If you have employees with a coordinated salary above CHF 21,150 annually, choose a professional pension fund in Aargau and register. Communicate the salary lists every year. For accident insurance (LAA), contact an insurance company competent in Aargau (usually SUVA or a private insurer) and insure your employees according to the activity sector.
Phase 9: Health insurance (LAMal) for employees
It is not the employer who registers the employees, but each employee personally takes out a LAMal policy with an insurer. It is your responsibility to inform employees of this obligation and, preferably, to communicate to them the cantonal premium comparators. You can offer a flat-rate contribution towards the premiums, but this is not mandatory by law.
### Tools to simplify the process
Use the [federal tax calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your IFD tax burden. Visit the Federal Customs Administration website for information on VAT and the identification number. Consult the Aargau Canton website (cantonal administration section) for specific cantonal procedures, official forms, and contact details of the relevant offices.
Do not underestimate the help of a Ticino or Aargau accountant or tax consultant: the cost of initial consultation (usually CHF 500-2,000 depending on complexity) is quickly offset by the taxes saved and the correct administrative management.

item.title: Wages and labour market in Schaffhausen
item.description: Swiss wage structure for training levels, collective agreements, social security system (AVS/LPP) and cantonal minimum wage. A practical guide to verifying your salary.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland; some cantons, including Schaffhausen, have defined it - Salary levels vary with the level of education (VET, high school, university) - Employee contributes 5.3% AVS/AI/IPG and LPP contributions proportional to age - Collective agreements set specific conditions for sector and company
## Key facts - **What**: Salary structure and Swiss labor market for education levels - Where: Canton of Schaffhausen and national Switzerland - Who: Employees, employers, SECO and cantonal statistical offices - Employee contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% + AD/AC 1.1% (annual maximum) - Maximum hours: 45 hours per week (industry/offices/sales) or 50 hours (other sectors) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks per year (5 for those under 20 years) - Education: VET, high school, university are the main drivers of wage differences
The Swiss labor market is characterized by strong wage differentiation linked to the level of education. There is no federal minimum wage, but the Canton of Schaffhausen and other cantons have defined their own minimum levels where applicable. Working conditions, including wages, are regulated by specific collective agreements for sector and company.
The Swiss education structure (VET, high school, university) is the main driver of wage differences. A worker with completed vocational training earns on average less than someone with a tertiary qualification. Additionally, the integrated pension system (AVS, LPP, third pillar) represents a significant part of the total remuneration, in addition to the gross salary.
### How are salaries structured in Switzerland
Salaries are not determined solely by the base, but by a complex system of mandatory contributions. The employee contributes 5.3% of the salary base for AVS (old-age), AI (disability) and IPG (loss of earnings compensation). In addition to this, they contribute to unemployment insurance (AD) and insolvency compensation (AC) with an additional 1.1%, up to an annual maximum set each year. A crucial aspect is the pension fund (LPP), where the employee contributes a percentage of the salary coordinated with rates for age bracket: 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54, 18% from 55 years until the reference age. Collective agreements, specific to the sector and often to the company, further define the salary level, seniority increases, bonuses, dismissal conditions and holidays. ## Training, pension and salary differentials
Training is the most determining factor in salary positioning. An apprenticeship completed with a federal certificate (AFC) opens access to modest initial salaries, which grow with seniority. A high school diploma or a post-compulsory specialization course represents a significant salary jump. A university degree or a polytechnic diploma places the worker at the highest salary levels, although the actual earnings depend on the employment sector.
The Canton of Schaffhausen, like all Swiss cantons, applies a three-level tax system: federal, cantonal and municipal. Each canton has its own multipliers, established by cantonal and municipal tax laws. A worker in Schaffhausen will have to calculate their tax burden considering all three rates. In addition to direct taxation, the employee bears non-negotiable mandatory pension costs. The pension fund LPP is managed by the employer and represents a substantial part of the total remuneration, as the company contributes an amount equal to the employee's contribution.
Furthermore, the employee must take out health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of starting work: it is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and the premiums vary by canton and region, with deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 annually, and often a premium reduction is available based on income.
### Comparative scenario: gross salaries and contributions
An employee with an AFC earns a lower gross salary than someone with tertiary education. For example, with a hypothetical gross salary in the entry-level range, the contribution for AVS/AI/IPG is the same by law (5.3%), but the absolute value in CHF is lower. An employee in the 45-54 age group pays 15% of their coordinated salary to the LPP, after deducting a federal minimum threshold (annually indexed). The tax burden depends on the canton: Schaffhausen and other cantons have their own rates and multipliers. The maximum working hours are 45 hours per week for industry, offices and sales; 50 hours for other sectors. The minimum holidays are 4 weeks per year (5 for those under 20), guaranteed by law. Maternity is covered with an allowance of 80% of the salary for 14 weeks (IPG), paternity with 2 paid weeks.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to check your salary and find data on the labor market
Before accepting a job offer or negotiating a contract renewal, it is essential to verify if your salary is aligned with market parameters. At the federal level, the SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) regularly publishes reports on the labor market situation, including data on unemployment, average salary levels by sector, and labor mobility. At the cantonal level, the statistical offices of Schaffhausen provide local data on salary structures. Collective agreements are a key element: consult the SECO website for a search of the collective agreements in force in your sector and canton.
If your employer applies a collective agreement, the salary is bound by those parameters; otherwise, it remains the result of individual negotiation. In the absence of a collective agreement, the employer is still required to comply with federal labor law and cantonal ordinances.
### Step-by-step: checking your salary
1. **Request the complete payslip**: it must indicate gross salary, deductions for AHV/AI/IPG (5.3%), AD/AC (1.1%), LPP, tax withholdings, and insurance. Compare the entries with the federal labor law.
2. Calculate the net take-home: use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the effect of federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation. Enter your canton of residence for an accurate estimate of the tax burden.
3. Check the collective agreement: if applicable, verify if your level of education corresponds to the salary bracket provided for your role.
4. Compare with average data: SECO and cantonal statistics provide median salaries by sector and level of education, useful for future negotiations.
5. Consult an expert: if you have doubts about deductions, LPP, or taxation, contact the cantonal labor office.
Remember that the total compensation includes not only the salary but also the employer's contributions to LPP, the value of health subsidies, and the right to 4-5 weeks of vacation. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) for a 360-degree view of your financial situation, considering taxation and pension together.

item.title: Schaffhausen transport subscriptions: zones and rates
item.description: Complete guide to public transport subscriptions in the canton of Schaffhausen: fare community, monthly and annual subscriptions, half-price, GA and student discounts.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Schaffhausen uses the system of Swiss tariff communities to coordinate railways and buses - Monthly and annual subscriptions are the most convenient solution for commuters - Half-price card saves up to 50% on national public networks - Students and apprentices benefit from significant discounts (15-50%)
## Key facts - **What**: Coordinated subscription system for fare zones in public transport - Where: Canton Schaffhausen, north-eastern Switzerland - Who: Residents, commuters, students and apprentices - When: Available all year round with automatic renewal - Types: Monthly, annual, half-price (50% discount), GA (unlimited national) - Model: Tariff community based on zoning of the territory
Canton Schaffhausen offers a full range of public mobility solutions, organized according to the Swiss standard tariff community model. Residents and commuters can choose from monthly or annual subscriptions, or combine national solutions such as half-price or GA subscription to maximize savings. The zonal structure guarantees transparency in tariffs and facilitates access to services for the entire population.
### How the Swiss tariff system works
In Switzerland, public transport is organized according to a federal model where each canton maintains autonomy over territorial management, but all adhere to coordinated pricing principles. ## Monthly vs. Annual Subscriptions: Which to Choose
The choice between a monthly and annual subscription depends directly on the frequency of use and the need for permanence. Those who commute daily within the canton of Schaffhausen for work or study purposes find convenience in the annual subscription: the pro-rata monthly cost is lower compared to the cost of 12 separate monthly subscriptions purchased individually. A common scenario is the commuter who chooses the annual subscription and amortizes the expense over 250 working days, drastically reducing the unit cost per trip.
Those who travel irregularly or have seasonal needs—temporary work, returns to other cantons, periods of smart working—should opt for the monthly subscription, with the freedom to cease renewal without penalties after the first month. Another significant element is the benefit from the employer. Many Swiss employers subsidize part of the annual subscription as a benefit, deducting a portion from the gross salary and completing the payment directly to the operator. This mechanism, widespread especially in regions with a high density of commuters such as urban belts, concretely reduces the cost of living for the worker and encourages sustainable mobility.
### Half-Price and GA: National Tools for Saving
Two national tools significantly expand the options for savings beyond the territorial subscription. The **half-fare card** (issued by the ARR—Swiss Association of Railway Companies) allows travel at a 50% reduced fare on every train and bus journey throughout Switzerland. It is not a territorial subscription but a universal discount applicable to any network. A resident of Schaffhausen who occasionally visits Zurich, Basel, or Geneva can subscribe to both their monthly cantonal subscription and the national half-fare card, paying the full price for local trips (already discounted by the zonal subscription) and enjoying a 50% reduction for national trips.
The GA (General-Abonnement) subscription represents the most comprehensive offer: unlimited access to all public networks in Switzerland for 365 consecutive days. It is particularly convenient for those who work in a canton different from their place of residence—for example, a resident of Schaffhausen who works in Zurich—since the fixed annual cost is lower compared to the cumulative purchase of canton A subscriptions + intra-cantonal travel zones + canton B subscription.
### Discounts for Students and Apprentices in Schaffhausen
Students and apprentices have access to reduced rates on monthly and annual subscriptions in the canton of Schaffhausen, as well as on the national network. The reductions vary slightly by operator but typically range between 15% and 50% off the standard adult subscription price. School certificates, high school enrollment certificates, or apprenticeship contracts legitimize the discount at the time of purchase. Some employers reimburse part of the subscription cost to apprentices as part of the training journey.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Purchase procedures and documentation
Residents and commuters of the canton of Schaffhausen can purchase subscriptions through multiple channels:
**Physical ticket offices**: SBB (Swiss Federal Railways) stations maintain counters in major stations. PostBus and local bus operators offer sales points at terminals and bus stops.
Authorized resellers: Newsstands, grocery stores, pharmacies, and gas stations have authorized ticket offices with access to cantonal subscriptions.
Digital platforms: Official apps and websites of operators allow online purchases, with pickup at designated counters in the following days or direct download of the digital card (for operators offering dematerialized passes).
The subscription renews automatically at the end of the period — monthly or annual — unless the user cancels it at least 15-30 days before the expiration date. Each operator and canton specifies precise cancellation times, easily consultable on the official website of the operator or at the counters.
### Documentation to access discounts
To benefit from student or apprentice discounts, it is necessary to present at the time of purchase:
- School enrollment certificate (students of public schools, high schools, universities) - Apprenticeship contract or professional school certificate (apprentices) - Identity card (for age verification and data consistency)
The documentation is presented at the physical counter or via upload on digital platforms if available. Spot checks can occur during onboard inspections to ensure the regularity of the status.
### Transportation and cost of living in Switzerland
The subscription is a significant element in the budget of those who live and work in Switzerland, as it represents one of the main components of the overall cost of living. According to data published by the FSO (Federal Statistical Office), public transport absorbs a considerable percentage of the monthly expenses of families and individuals, varying according to the frequency of use. Choosing the correct type of subscription — distinguishing between monthly, annual, half-price, and GA — and combining it strategically with employer subsidies significantly reduces the expense burden. To calculate potential savings and compare options based on your travel profile, it is useful to consult [dedicated cost of living tools](nav:cost-of-living) and [guides on Swiss public transport](nav:transport) available online.

item.title: Swiss companies, half-year results beyond estimates
item.description: In the first half of the year, 24 out of 30 companies in the SLI index exceeded market expectations. 2026 profit estimates revised to +18% thanks to investments in artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - In the first half of the year, 24 out of 30 SLI companies exceeded market estimates - Logitech beat operating profit forecasts by 39% - Investments in artificial intelligence main drivers of growth - Revised 2026 profit estimates up 18%
## Key facts - **What**: Financial results for Swiss companies in the first half exceed market expectations - When: First semester - Where: Swiss Stock Exchange, SLI index (30 listed companies) - Who: 24 companies above estimates, 4 below forecasts - Logitech Performance: Operating profit +39% compared to estimates - Givaudan Performance: Net profit -12% compared to estimates - ABB performance: Net profit -7% compared to estimates
Twenty-four large Swiss companies out of thirty surprisingly exceeded market expectations in the first half, demonstrating a financial solidity that analysts had not fully anticipated. According to Keystone-ATS, this performance comes despite a complicated geopolitical context: war in the Middle East, rising oil prices, US tariffs and a particularly strong Swiss franc on international markets.
Bettina Baur, manager of the private bank UBP, points out that "the results shown by companies in the first half are clearly above average and the magnitude of the surprises was remarkable". Among the most egregious successes, the luxury giant Richemont has doubled its sales growth compared to analysts' forecasts. ### Stock market volatility and its impact on investors
The stock market reaction has been particularly lively. Stocks have seen significant fluctuations of up to 10% more or less on the day of the publication of the reports. Gauthier explains that "the concentration in the publication of corporate information is very, very high, which causes excessive reactions from the market." On some days, ten companies simultaneously released their results, putting the investors' ability to process information to the test.
The high volatility is also fueled by the behavior of small speculators. Many take leveraged positions and close them at the first significant deviation from expectations. "Moreover, many speculators follow the trend, take leveraged positions, and at the slightest deviation from expectations, the positions are adjusted: this is what creates this incredible volatility, even on large-cap stocks," explains the expert.
For those who own stocks or funds in Switzerland (including [pension funds LPP/BVG](nav:pension)), this means that the value of the portfolio can fluctuate significantly in a few days. However, the overall context remains generally positive. Baur observes a "recovery of quality stocks, which were previously under strong pressure."
### Outlook for 2026 and beyond
The prospects for the second half of 2026 remain solid. According to Gauthier, "industrial companies should continue to report solid results in the second half of the year, as demand remains very strong despite inflation and rising interest rates." However, a change is already on the horizon: starting in early 2027, there could be a slowdown.
A particularly significant data point is the upward revision of corporate profit growth estimates for 2026. At the beginning of the year, specialists predicted an acceleration of 10%; meanwhile, the estimates have been revised upwards to 18%. This means that the return expectations for shareholders and Swiss pension fund members are expanding.
Those who wish to invest independently beyond the mandatory pension fund can consider the [third pillar 3a](nav:pillar3), which offers tax advantages and the possibility to choose the investment mix based on their risk profile and time horizon.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to do as a saver or investor in Switzerland
If you own shares in Swiss companies or if your pension fund is invested in Swiss equities, it is important to understand that the macroeconomic framework remains favorable. However, stock market volatility requires awareness and planning.
Step 1: Assess your exposure to Swiss companies. If you have a pension fund managed by a Swiss bank or insurance company, most of it is probably exposed to SMI/SLI index stocks. Ask your manager what percentage of the portfolio is invested in Swiss stocks and what in bonds or foreign assets.
Step 2: Understand the mix of your allocation. For those who are young (more than 10 years from retirement), an exposure of 60-70% in equities may be appropriate; for those approaching retirement, it may be reduced to 30-40%. Review your LPP/BVG account statement to verify the strategic allocation and management costs.
Step 3: Do not react emotionally to daily volatility. Variations of 10% are normal in weeks of results publication, but they represent short-term movements. If your plan is long-term (retirement in 10 or more years), it is not advisable to sell to fix losses during temporary declines. History shows that diversified portfolios recover during economic cycles.
Step 4: Monitor the evolution for 2027. Given that analysts predict a possible slowdown starting in January 2027, it is reasonable to start thinking about a possible portfolio rebalancing a few months before. Consult your financial advisor or your [bank to discuss investment management strategies](nav:banks).

item.title: Buying a house in Zurich: mortgage, own funds and taxes
item.description: Procedure, financing and tax charges for the purchase of a house in the Canton of Zurich: mortgage loan, own funds, transfer tax and notary fees.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Purchasing a home requires own funds generally equal to 20% of the value - The mortgage is the main financing tool in Switzerland - Transfer tax and notary fees vary by canton and affect the total cost - The federal procedure involves evaluation, sustainability check, notarial deed
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of real estate with a mortgage - Where: Canton of Zurich (standardized Swiss federal procedure) - Legal instrument: Swiss Civil Code, cantonal regulations on taxes and registration - Who: Bank (evaluation/mortgage disbursement), notary, cantonal administration - Deadlines: From the promise of purchase to the notarial deed: 4–8 weeks
Buying a house in the Canton of Zurich follows a standardized federal procedure, although taxes and fees vary significantly by cantonal and municipal jurisdiction. The process revolves around three pillars: the availability of sufficient own funds, access to mortgage credit, and coverage of ancillary costs (transfer taxes, notary fees, registration).
Unlike many European jurisdictions, Switzerland does not set a single federal minimum wage—hence, banks assess the sustainability of real estate debt based on standardized criteria linked to repayment capacity and personal financial portfolio. The three-tier tax structure (federal, cantonal, municipal) means that property transfer taxes and administrative fees change radically depending on the jurisdiction.
### Real estate financing: mortgage and own funds
The standard Swiss practice requires the buyer to have own funds equal to at least 20% of the property value; the remaining 80% is covered by a mortgage. Some banks are stricter and require 25–30%, especially if the income is not stable or the borrower is an individual with limited credit history in Switzerland.
The mortgage is a secured loan registered in the land register. The bank acquires a lien on the property until the full repayment of the capital and interest. Interest rates vary based on the bank's yield rate determined by the Swiss National Bank (SNB), the amortization period (generally 15–30 years), and the borrower's risk profile.
Before granting the mortgage, the bank orders a professional evaluation of the property to ensure that the real value covers at least the loaned capital. This evaluation is mandatory and involves costs borne by the buyer.
### Sustainability check: the bank's stress test
Swiss banks apply the so-called "stress test": a calculation that verifies whether the borrower could pay the installments even at higher interest rates than the current ones. The calculation includes: - Declared gross annual income - Family burdens and other debt obligations - Monthly mortgage installment amount (principal + interest) - Estimated annual maintenance costs and taxes - Mandatory fire insurance for mortgaged properties
A conventional ratio accepted by banks is: the sum of all monthly installments (mortgage + other debts + taxes + insurance) should not exceed 33% of the gross monthly income. Those acquiring a house must also take out health insurance (LAMal/KVG), mandatory for all Swiss residents within 3 months of arrival, which represents a recurring expense affecting the ability to sustain the mortgage. ### Personal financial sustainability
The bank will calculate the sustainability of the mortgage according to conventional criteria, but the prudent buyer must personally assess the financial situation. A crucial aspect: the monthly mortgage payment added to all other debt obligations must not exceed 33% of the gross monthly income according to banking standards. If the situation is at the limit of this ratio, a subsequent rise in interest rates will put pressure on the personal budget.
It is not enough to have 20% of own funds to buy a house. You must have a stable and documented income. If you are married, the partner's income counts, but only if demonstrably stable; if you work as a self-employed person, the bank checks are more rigorous and require multi-year income certificates.
### The role of pension and cantonal taxation
Anyone working in Switzerland pays mandatory contributions to the pension system: AVS/AHV (pension), AI (disability), IPG (maternity allowance), AD and AC (unemployment), LPP (second pillar, company pension fund). Each contribution represents a deduction from gross income and affects the availability of free income to pay the mortgage.
The Swiss tax structure operates at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal. The federal direct tax (IFD) is progressive and national; cantonal and municipal taxes vary significantly. A property owner in Zurich pays ordinary property taxes different from other cantons. Mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is a recurring expense (monthly or annual premiums) that reduces available income.
### Transfer taxes and ancillary charges
When buying a property in Switzerland, the transfer of ownership is not taxed at the federal level (there is no VAT on used properties). However, the purchase incurs two main types of cantonal and municipal charges:
Transfer tax: Each canton has its own laws. Some cantons tax capital gains (profit between purchase price and sale price), others apply a fixed tax on the transaction, others still use progressive brackets based on the value of the property. In the Canton of Zurich, the rate and specific mechanism are established by cantonal law and vary depending on price ranges and property category. It is essential to verify directly with the cantonal tax office before signing the preliminary contract, as the amount significantly impacts the total budget.
Notary fees: The notarial deed is mandatory by federal law (Civil Code). The notary verifies identity, validity of the title, absence of pre-existing liens, and drafts the deed in public form. The cost is generally between 0.5% and 1.5% of the purchase value according to cantonal rates.
In addition to these, there are also the costs of registration in the land register (cadastre), generally low. Once purchased, the property is subject to annual cantonal/municipal property taxes (wealth tax). This is NOT the same as the transfer tax, but a recurring tribute on resident owners, variable by canton and municipality.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete procedure: from interest to acquisition
Phase 1: Financial preparation (2–6 months in advance) Verify your gross income and that of your partner (if applicable). Gather documents: pay slips from the last 12 months, IFD statements, employment certificates, list of existing debts. Calculate your available own funds (personal savings, inheritance, possible withdrawals from the second pillar LPP — but with awareness of federal constraints). Schedule a meeting with a bank or mortgage advisor for an informal pre-qualification.
Phase 2: Property search and offer (1–4 months) Browse local and national Swiss real estate portals. Once you have identified a property, submit a purchase offer (non-binding, but marks your interest). Request a preliminary valuation of the property.
Phase 3: Formal commitment and evaluation (1–2 months) Sign a purchase agreement with the seller (legally binding document, subject to financing approval). Send the agreement and financial documents to the bank. The bank orders a professional valuation and communicates the decision within 2–4 weeks.
Phase 4: Notarial deed and registration (2–4 weeks before closing) Contact the notary to set the date for the public deed. The notary verifies the titles with the land registry and prepares the deed. One week before signing, you receive a final estimate of all costs. Crucial moment: verify with the cantonal tax office the exact amount of the transfer tax.
Phase 5: Signing and property transfer (closing day) You, the seller, the notary, and bank representatives meet to sign the deed. The transfer of funds occurs (own funds + mortgage disbursement from the bank account to the notary). The deed is authenticated by the notary and transmitted to the land registry for registration.
Phase 6: Land registry registration and closing (1–2 weeks after) The land registry registers the transfer and the new mortgage in favor of the bank. The bank communicates the registration and transfers the money to the seller. You are now the registered owner of the property.
### Practical tools and final checks
Before signing the contract, verify with: - Affordability calculator: many banks offer online tools where you enter the price, own funds, and income to receive an estimate of the monthly installment and a preliminary judgment - Mortgage rate comparator: independent sites compare rates and conditions between banks - **Zurich cantonal tax office**: find out the exact rate of the transfer tax in the municipality of your interest
For further insight into how your repayment capacity is distributed between mortgage, pension (AVS/LPP), health insurance (LAMal), and federal/cantonal taxes, use our [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator). This will allow you to clearly see which portion of your gross income remains available for mortgage installments after all mandatory deductions.

item.title: One in two summers will be warmer than the current one
item.description: According to climatologist Reto Knutti, one in two summers will be warmer than the current one. Urgent interventions needed in cities.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - One summer in two will be hotter than the current one. - Health risks and more linked to extreme heat and drought. - Urgent interventions needed on cities.
## Key facts - **What**: Future climate prospects in Switzerland. - When: Next years. - Where: Switzerland. - Who: Reto Knutti, climatologist at ETH. - Amount: Estimated economic losses of half a billion francs or more per year.
Zurich - As Switzerland prepares to face a new heatwave in the coming days, climatologist Reto Knutti warns about future prospects. "With current global climate policies, we are heading towards a world where one summer in two will be hotter than this one," says the professor of climate physics at ETH in an interview published today by Watson.
According to Knutti, the exceptional heat of the summer of 2026 is not surprising compared to the scenarios developed by MeteoSwiss and ETH. Five factors contribute to this: global warming, responsible for 60-70% in his opinion, soil drought, cleaner air and the consequent greater solar radiation, the accumulation of high pressures over Europe, and the scarcity of thunderstorms. The expert also recalls that Basel and Sion recorded over 50 days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees at the measuring stations this year.
The effects, he points out, are already heavy. Knutti speaks of hundreds of additional deaths in Switzerland this summer due to the heat and at least 35,000 victims in Europe. The drought is also worrying: agriculture has suffered, while damage to forests may only become apparent later. The heat would also have repercussions on psychological health and productivity, with losses in Switzerland estimated by the expert at half a billion francs or more per year.
### Impact on health and economy
Extreme heat and drought not only put people's health at risk but also have a significant impact on the economy. Knutti emphasizes that the estimated economic losses in Switzerland could reach half a billion francs or more per year. This includes not only direct health costs but also productivity losses and damage to agriculture and forests.
### Urgent interventions needed
To address the situation, according to the professor, it is necessary to rethink especially cities and buildings, intervening in spatial planning, increasing greenery, and adopting the concept of "sponge city," capable of retaining water and releasing it through evaporation. Air conditioning will also have to enter the debate, particularly for nursing homes, public buildings, and schools: "Air conditioners prevent victims, it is absolutely clear," he says, while specifying that this does not mean equipping every home.
Knutti specifies that climate change is not a future problem and we must prepare especially for heat and drought. Adaptation, however, "has limits or becomes prohibitively expensive": for this, he concludes, the reduction of emissions must also have the same priority. ## Practical analysis: concrete implications at national/cantonal level
Knutti's forecasts have concrete implications for Switzerland. Swiss cities will face significant challenges in adapting to climate change. Spatial planning and increased urban greenery will be crucial to mitigate the effects of extreme heat and drought.
### Spatial planning and urban greenery
The «sponge city» is a concept that could become fundamental for Swiss cities. This strategy involves the use of porous materials and the creation of green spaces that can retain water and reduce the risk of flooding. In addition, urban greenery can help cool cities, improving air quality and the health of residents.
### Air conditioning: a partial solution
Air conditioning could be a partial solution to dealing with extreme heat, especially in public buildings and retirement homes. However, Knutti stresses that it is not a universal solution and that it should be used with caution, also considering the environmental impact of air conditioners.
### Emissions reduction
Although adaptation is necessary, Knutti recalls that reducing emissions must have the same priority. This means that climate policies globally need to be reviewed and strengthened to avoid a future where one in two summers will be warmer than the current one.

## In brief - The Swiss franc falls against the euro. - It reaches a one-year low. - Interest rate differential between Switzerland and the Eurozone.
## Key facts - **What**: The Swiss franc falls against the euro. - When: Today. - Where: Switzerland. - Who: Swiss National Bank (SNB), European Central Bank (ECB). - Amount: 0.9435 francs per euro.
The Swiss franc continues to weaken against the euro, a trend that has been noticeable for days. Today, the European currency reached a high of 0.9435 francs, a level not seen since August 2025.
Experts attribute this phase of weakness in the Swiss currency primarily to the interest rate differential between Switzerland and the Eurozone. The currency trend may seem paradoxical in an international context that is still tense, but it is mainly explained by the sudden return of the interest rate theme to the forefront, explains John Plassard, the investment strategy manager at the bank Cité Gestion. "It is not Switzerland (and its safe-haven currency) that is suddenly inspiring less confidence, but the euro that is regaining an advantage in terms of yield that it had largely lost in recent years."
The gap between the Swiss National Bank's (SNB) key rate, currently at 0.00%, and the European Central Bank's (ECB) rate, at 2.25%, makes investments in euros more profitable than those in francs. With inflation in the Eurozone reaching 3.3% in August, a more restrictive monetary policy from the ECB is also on the horizon. "The market already considers a move to a deposit rate of 2.50% as a given, and, above all, is beginning to wonder how long Frankfurt will have to maintain this stricter line," comments Plassard.
### Implications for investors
The next two weeks will be crucial for monetary policy. Both the ECB and the Federal Reserve will decide on this. While an increase in the cost of money is certain in the Eurozone, the situation in the United States is not yet entirely clear, although expectations of a rate hike have increased. For its part, the SNB will present its assessment of the situation on September 24: analysts predict that the institution led by Martin Schlegel will opt for the status quo. ## Practical analysis
The weakening of the Swiss franc against the euro has significant implications for investors and the Swiss economy. The rate differential between Switzerland and the Eurozone makes investments in euros more attractive, as they offer higher returns than those in francs. This phenomenon could lead to an increase in investments in euros, with potential consequences for the Swiss financial market.
### Impact on inflation
Inflation in the Eurozone reached 3.3% in August, which could lead to tighter monetary policy by the ECB. An increase in the deposit rate to 2.50% is already considered discounted by the market. This scenario could influence the decisions of the SNB, which could keep its lead rate at 0.00% to avoid further pressure on the Swiss economy.
### Future scenarios
The upcoming decisions of the ECB and the Federal Reserve will be crucial in determining the trend of interest rates and, consequently, the value of the Swiss franc. Analysts expect the SNB to maintain the status quo, but the market will continue to closely monitor central banks' moves to assess the potential repercussions on the Swiss economy.

item.title: Apprenticeship in the Canton of Zurich: a practical guide
item.description: How to find an internship, understand the apprenticeship contract, salaries and professional maturity in the Canton of Zurich.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Swiss apprenticeship: integrated dual system (school + company), typical duration 3-4 years - Canton Zurich: one of the main training hubs with a consistent offer of internships - Mandatory written contract with specific rights: increasing salary per year, 5 weeks under-20 holidays - Professional maturity: certification parallel to the apprenticeship that accesses the SUPs
## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training system (company + vocational school) with binding contract - Where: Canton Zurich (applicable in all cantons according to uniform federal law) - When: Duration 3-4 years, starting at 15-16 years post-secondary - Who: Post-compulsory young people; registered training companies; cantonal vocational schools - Rights: Increasing salary per year, legal protection CO art. 344 ff., AVS/AI contributions, 5 weeks under-20 holidays
Apprenticeship in Switzerland is the most common training path for young people after middle school. In the Canton of Zurich, the system works according to the federal dual model: each apprentice alternates days at the training company with days of vocational school, acquiring both practical and theoretical skills. The standard duration is 3-4 years, depending on the business address.
Throughout the course, a written apprenticeship contract governs rights and duties. The company undertakes to train according to federal requirements and sectoral standards; ### Finding an internship in the Canton of Zurich
The offer of traineeships in the Canton of Zurich is published on federal and cantonal platforms managed by professional associations. The main resources are the national brokerage portals (YOUSTY, LENA and similar), where each company registered as a trainer publishes annually the available positions by sector.
The Cantonal Vocational Guidance Office of the Canton of Zurich collects information on places, carries out individual counselling for young people and provides data on training companies active in the territory. In addition, trade unions and professional associations for specific sectors (construction, electronics, commerce, hospitality, agriculture) publish dedicated offers.
The research should begin 12-18 months before the end of middle school. Young people spontaneously send applications to training companies, attaching school report card, motivational letter, personal curriculum. Selection interviews and short aptitude tests at the company often follow.
### The apprenticeship contract: rights and obligations
The binding contract stipulated between apprentice (and parents if minor), training company and competent cantonal office contains elements standardized by federal law:
- ** Total duration ** of the apprenticeship (example: 3 years, 4 years) - Professional sector and Federal Certificate of Competence number (AFC — Certificate of Vocational Training) - Monthly salary
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The professional maturity: parallel certification to the apprenticeship
An even more attractive path is the **professional maturity** (PM), a federal certification that can be obtained parallel to the apprenticeship without extending the overall duration of the training. The PM allows direct access to professional universities (PU — Fachhochschulen) without requiring an additional year of complementary training.
In the Canton of Zurich, vocational schools offer professional maturity modules integrated into the apprenticeship curriculum, typically with 1-2 additional lessons per week. Access to the PM depends on school performance during the apprenticeship: educational institutions evaluate aptitudes in mathematics, languages, and technical subjects. The consequence of the PM is a federal certificate that certifies both professional skills and academic preparation.
### Step-by-step procedure to start
Phase 1 — Orientation and research (months 10-12 of middle school)
Consult the cantonal orientation office of the Canton of Zurich, participate in professional fairs and school orientation days, discuss with parents and teachers, identify 5-10 realistic sectors of interest based on personal aptitudes and local market.
Phase 2 — Active application (months 18-6 before the end of middle school)
Regularly visit federal portals of internship offers (YOUSTY, LENA, professional association websites), write a concise CV and personalized motivational letter, contact training companies directly in the chosen sector, participate in informative meetings and company open days, prepare for aptitude tests and selection interviews.
Phase 3 — Negotiation and contract signing (months 3 before the start of the apprenticeship)
Receive and evaluate the binding internship offer, sign the contract (parents will sign if underage), deposit the contract with the competent cantonal office, receive the official administrative confirmation and the summons for the first day of work.
Phase 4 — Start of the apprenticeship
The first day of work marks the beginning of the trial period (3 months). During this period, both the apprentice and the company can terminate without notice and without special justification. At the end of the trial period, the contract becomes fully binding for both parties until the completion of the path.
### Practical tools to deepen and compare opportunities
To evaluate your estimated salary as an apprentice in the Canton of Zurich and compare the evolution of remuneration in different years, use the salary calculator. A tool that estimates the gross and net amount based on the professional sector and canton of work.
Additionally, consult the [job and apprenticeship offers](nav:jobs) regularly published: many companies release new internship positions in predictable cycles during the school year. The investment in professional training pays off concretely: apprentices who complete the path access the job market with federal certificates recognized throughout Switzerland, defined career prospects in the specific profession, and access to further continuing education (specialization courses, professional maturity, higher education).

item.description: Novartis announces the cut of up to 130 jobs in Basel by the end of 2027. Reason: transfer of activities to Novartis Campus and expiration of contracts.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Novartis to cut up to 130 jobs by the end of 2027 in Basel - Reason: expiration of Kleinbasel contracts, transfer to Novartis Campus - Since 2018: nearly 3,000 layoffs by Novartis in Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Job cuts in low-volume biologics production - When: By the end of 2027 - Where: Basel, Kleinbasel district - Who: Novartis (pharmaceutical group) - Number: Up to 130 jobs
Novartis announces the cut of up to 130 jobs at its Basel site. The decision was communicated on Wednesday by the Swiss pharmaceutical group and will take effect by the end of 2027. Due to the expiration of lease contracts in the Kleinbasel district, the production of low-volume biologics will be abandoned at the current site. This is part of a broader production reorganization strategy that Novartis has been pursuing for years.
The biological production activities will not completely disappear from Basel: they will be transferred to other production sites worldwide. Meanwhile, several divisions will transfer their operations from the Kleinbasel district to the Novartis Campus, located on the other side of the Rhine. Among the activities involved are laboratories for biological cell banks, analytical testing procedures, and offices dedicated to technical development.
This transfer represents the continuation of previously announced plans to build a new center specializing in the technical development of biologics at the campus. This center will integrate with the existing biologics research center within the structure.
### Consultation and social plan All planned changes are subject to the information and consultation process. Novartis is committed to supporting the affected employees with a series of offers, including a long-term social plan. This support will be discussed and negotiated during the consultation phase with worker representatives.
The consultation process is a critical moment for the affected employees: it allows them to negotiate the terms of the restructuring and to explore alternative options to layoffs. During this phase, unions will play a crucial role in protecting workers' interests. ### A worrying trend for Swiss employment
The announcement by Novartis comes nine months after the previous major job cut in Stein, in Aargau. Since 2018, the group has eliminated nearly 3,000 jobs in Switzerland. This figure reflects a corporate restructuring strategy that has been ongoing for years and significantly impacts the Swiss job market.
The cuts since 2018 represent a total of nearly 3,000 lost jobs. The Swiss pharmaceutical sector is directly affected by the loss of qualified employment in companies of the caliber of Novartis. Restructuring in large companies indirectly influences the local economy and cantonal social services.
### The position of the unions
The union Unia has expressed "alarm at the continued dismantling of production jobs in Switzerland." The union's request is clear: Novartis should refrain from layoffs and ensure the continuation of employment for workers at another site in northwestern Switzerland, rather than transferring production abroad.
This position highlights the issue of relocation: the transfer of production to other countries raises doubts about the long-term effects on Switzerland's productive capacity. For workers directly affected, negotiation during the consultation phase will be crucial to obtain the maximum possible support. item.title: PA 2030+: more freedom for Swiss farmers
item.description: The Federal Council launches consultation on PA30+: management autonomy, less bureaucracy, digitalisation and CHF 13.8 billion of investment for agriculture 2030-2033.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council launches PA30+ consultation until December 8 - More management autonomy for farmers, less bureaucracy - Spending 2030-2033: 13.8 billion CHF (-123 million vs 2026-2029)
## Key facts - **What**: Agricultural Policy 2030+ with 4 areas of intervention - When: Consultation until December 8; in force 2030-2033 - Where: Switzerland (all cantons) - Who: Federal Council, farmers, traders, consumers - Amount: 13.8 billion CHF for 2030-2033
The Federal Council today announced the Agricultural Policy 2030+ (PA30+), a new regulatory framework for the Swiss agricultural sector aimed at increasing national food security by expanding farmers' operational leeway. The consultation remains open until December 8.
"The actors in the agri-food chain and consumers are called upon to take on greater responsibilities to ensure an ecologically, economically, and socially sustainable food system," the executive explained in a statement. Federal President Guy Parmelin outlined the details during a press conference.
### The four strategic areas of PA30+
The PA30+ is structured around four strategic areas. The first concerns the expansion of farmers' operational leeway and the reduction of administrative burden through digitalization. Currently, direct payments to farmers are closely linked to compliance with certain prescriptions. With PA30+, these payments will increasingly be linked to the actual results achieved, offering greater management freedom.
To support this transition, the Federal Council intends to substantially raise the entry thresholds for direct payments in the lowland and hilly zones, as well as for structural improvements in the lowland zone. "In this way, we aim to reduce costs and ask farmers to find synergies among themselves," Parmelin explained.
The second area concerns the proper functioning of markets. The executive intends to strengthen market observation and extend solidarity measures to help agricultural businesses value their products and strengthen their position in the domestic market. Additional specific support is also planned for the dairy sector and for crops directly intended for human consumption, with the aim of improving farmers' economic situation.
The third area addresses crop protection. Measures are planned to promote beneficial insects and organisms in biological control, support the development of sustainable technologies, and strengthen training and advice for farmers. In this way, agricultural businesses will receive greater support in adapting to climate change.
The last area concerns the involvement of retail trade and consumers. The government intends to promote sustainability throughout the value chain through agreements on objectives with traders and greater awareness among citizens towards Swiss products. This approach aims to positively influence the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) through a more transparent supply chain. ### How agricultural payments are changing
The Federal Council intends to submit to Parliament the spending limits for agriculture for the period 2030-2033, for a total of 13.8 billion francs. This amount represents a reduction of 123 million francs compared to the previous period (2026-2029), but still an increase of 80 million compared to what would be available if the 2030 financial plan were maintained at nominal values.
The reduction compared to the previous three-year period reflects the efficiency objective of PA30+: through the reduction of administrative burden and the strengthening of digitalization, the system aims to achieve the same support for the sector with slightly lower costs. However, compared to a scenario of simple continuity, PA30+ represents an additional investment of 80 million.
One of the most significant changes concerns the shift from payments linked to compliance with prescriptions to payments linked to results. This system offers farmers greater flexibility in choosing the operational methods to achieve sustainability, environmental protection, and food safety goals.
The increase in entry thresholds for direct payments, particularly in the plains and hills, represents a structural incentive to promote aggregations and synergies between companies. Smaller companies could associate to meet the required thresholds, allowing them to access direct payments and structural improvements. This mechanism reduces the fragmentation of the sector and promotes economies of scale.
### The central role of the Swiss consumer
PA30+ recognizes that the end consumer plays a crucial role in supporting the sustainable food system. Through agreements on objectives with traders and awareness of Swiss products, it is intended to create a positive dynamic that connects agricultural supply with conscious consumer demand.
This shift from the supply side to a multi-stakeholder approach (farmers, traders, consumers, institutions) represents a paradigm shift in how Switzerland manages food security. It is no longer just about subsidizing production, but about building an ecosystem where all actors share responsibilities and benefits.

The consultation on PA30+ remains open until December 8. This period is intended to collect feedback from farmers, industry associations, traders, environmental organizations, and interested citizens.
Those wishing to contribute can submit observations and proposals directly to the Federal Council. The specific methods of participation (format of observations, transmission addresses, possible regional information meetings) must be verified on the official website of the Swiss government or with the cantonal agricultural administrations, which often facilitate the dialogue between their farmers and the federal consultation.
### Practical implications for the agricultural sector
For farmers, PA30+ represents a concrete opportunity to reduce bureaucracy. The digitization of the application and monitoring processes for direct payments should significantly simplify administrative management, freeing up time and resources for production activities. At the same time, the increase in entry thresholds represents a stimulus to rethink the organizational structure: associations between small farms, cooperatives, or sharing of infrastructure could offer new [employment opportunities](nav:jobs) and synergies in the sector.
For traders, the agreements on objectives with the Federal Council represent a shared framework for promoting Swiss agricultural products. This creates opportunities for differentiation and marketing linked to sustainability, strengthening the connection between conscious consumers and local quality supply.
### Next steps and time horizon
The presentation to Parliament of the spending limits will take place after the conclusion of the consultation, probably in 2027. Parliamentary approval will be necessary before PA30+ can fully enter into force for the period 2030-2033.
In the meantime, farmers and sector operators should stay informed about the developments of the consultation. Contacting the cantonal professional agricultural associations and following the official channels of the Federal Council allows you to keep up with the news.
For those who need information on the current direct payments to farmers, on the structure of federal subsidies, and on the calculation of the contributions that will benefit from the new thresholds, it is advisable to consult the dedicated federal support and information services.

item.title: Switzerland less attractive to multinationals: McKinsey alarm
item.description: 70% of CEOs warn that Switzerland is losing competitiveness. Criticisms of lengthy procedures, OECD tax and poor infrastructure threaten foreign investment.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 70% of CEOs believe Switzerland is losing international appeal - Main criticisms: lengthy procedures (70%), OECD minimum tax (65%), inadequate infrastructure (60%) - Multinationals generate 42% of Swiss GDP, despite being 6% of businesses
## Key facts - **What**: Study on Switzerland's loss of appeal for multinationals - When: Published today - Who: McKinsey and Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce - Amount: 70% CEOs convinced of the loss; 42% GDP from multinationals; 6% multinational businesses - Criticisms: Procedures (+70%), OECD tax (+65%), infrastructure (+60%)
Seven out of ten business leaders are convinced that the Swiss economic hub is losing its advantages compared to international competition. The alarm was sounded by a study published by the consulting firm McKinsey and the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce. According to the report, the Confederation remains the leading European hub for research and development but attracts fewer global company headquarters and fewer international executives than in the past. 70% of the CEOs surveyed believe that Switzerland is taking steps backward regarding its international appeal.
### Main criticisms Three specific areas concentrate managerial complaints. The lengthening of approval procedures for investment projects and work permits for foreign talent was reported by 70% of respondents. The introduction of the OECD minimum tax concerns 65%, while infrastructure bottlenecks are highlighted by 60%.
According to the managers interviewed, geopolitical tensions, new trade barriers, uncertainty in relations with the European Union, and the strength of the franc also weigh on perception.
### The crucial role of multinationals Multinationals play an essential role in the Swiss economy. Although they represent only 6% of businesses in Switzerland, they generate 42% of Swiss GDP and are the source of three-quarters of nominal economic growth since 2014. Losing competitiveness in this segment would have significant repercussions on employment, territorial development, and overall country growth. ## What does this loss mean for those working in Switzerland?
### Implications for economic growth
The contraction of attractiveness mentioned by McKinsey is not purely a statistical phenomenon. Since 2014, multinational companies have generated three-quarters of Switzerland's nominal economic growth. If this positive dynamic were to reverse, overall investments, salary opportunities, and direct and indirect jobs would slow down. This is not a remote risk: the report explicitly states that the Confederation is already attracting fewer global company headquarters and fewer international executives than in the past.
### The three knots to untie
Three specific factors require urgent intervention, according to the opinion of CEOs. Approval procedures for investments and work permits have become slower—a critical issue highlighted by 70% of respondents. The imposition of the OECD minimum tax was perceived as a competitive burden by 65% of managers. And infrastructure, from energy to transportation, shows structural bottlenecks (noted by 60%).
[Discover how to monitor job opportunities in Switzerland](nav:jobs).
### Balance between regulation and competitiveness
A critical point of the McKinsey report: a strong economic hub is not built through wild deregulation. It requires "efficient, proportionate, and predictable framework conditions that allow for innovation, investment, and growth." This means that Switzerland does not have to choose between regulatory rigor and attractiveness but must find a balance that allows international businesses to operate with legal certainty and administrative speed.
### The context of geopolitical pressure
In addition to the structural issues of regulation and taxation, McKinsey and the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce highlight the role of global geopolitical tensions, new trade barriers, and uncertainty in relations between Switzerland and the European Union. This is compounded by the volatility of the Swiss franc, which affects currency competitiveness for multinational companies operating in euros and dollars. These external factors amplify the damage caused by internal structural weaknesses.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to reverse the trend: the five-axis plan
### The pillars of the strategy according to McKinsey
The report identifies five priority areas to preserve the country's attractiveness in the long term, and their implementation will require coordination between the Confederation and the cantons. The first is to ensure access to international talent, accelerating work permits and making the country attractive to foreign professionals. The second is to streamline regulatory procedures, reducing authorization times for projects and investments. The third is to build fiscal predictability, clearly communicating how Switzerland will implement the OECD minimum tax and avoiding tax surprises. The fourth is to invest in infrastructure, especially in mobility, energy, and telecommunications. The fifth is to define a coherent strategic positioning towards the European Union, the United States, and Asia.
### Who decides what: the distribution of responsibilities
The responsibility for reversing the trend is distributed among multiple levels of government. The procedures for granting work permits (category L for short-term, B for residence, C for domicile, G for cross-border commuters) depend on the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and the cantonal authorities. The implementation of the OECD minimum tax is a federal competence, following international directives. Infrastructure involves both the Confederation and the cantons. Strategic coherence towards the United States, the European Union, and Asia is the responsibility of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. There is no single "lever" to pull: effective coordination between levels is needed.
### How to follow the progress
Frontaliere Ticino recommends monitoring the next McKinsey reports and observing the data from the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) on new multinational settlements and work permits issued. The Federal Statistical Office (FSO) also publishes data on economic growth and the contribution of multinationals to national GDP. These tools allow evaluating whether federal and cantonal policies are effectively reversing the loss of competitiveness signaled by the study.
